extracted.intended_audience: students, writers, and general readers interested in literary genres and genre theory
extracted.subtask_description: Explaining how literary works are categorized into genres and subgenres, including the criteria (technique, tone, content, length), historical theories (Aristotle, Frye), and related narrative elements and forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-determination criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Genres may be determined by literary technique, tone, content, or length (especially for fiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these axes (technique, tone, content, length) to group works; note that these bases can overlap and a work may fit multiple genres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility and instability of genre boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinctions between genres and categories are flexible and loosely defined, and even the rules designating genres change over time and are fairly unstable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect boundary cases, hybrid works, and historical change; do not treat genre labels as absolute prescriptions for composition or evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form-based classification (prose/poetry/drama)
rubrics_metrics.description: Western literature is typically subdivided into the classic three forms: poetry, drama, and prose; each can be further subdivided (e.g., lyric, epic, dramatic poetry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify first by major literary form, then by subgenre within that form using structure, length, and performance mode as discriminators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical-purpose genres (Aristotle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle proposed three literary genres of rhetorical oratory: deliberative (argue for future policy/action), forensic (discuss past action), and epideictic (offer praise or blame during a ceremony).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categorize oratory and rhetorical works by their persuasive purpose when assigning genre; this axis emphasizes function rather than form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic genres & rules of construction (Aristotle's Poetics)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Poetics Aristotle divided poetry into epic, tragedy, and comedy based on a combination of structure, content and narrative form, and proposed definitions and rules for each type's construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating poetic works consider how they conform to or deviate from the classical structural/content rules associated with each poetic genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgenre nesting and specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Genres are divided into subgenres (e.g., the novel → detective novel → 'hard-boiled' detective novel), producing hierarchies of increasingly specific categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use nested subgenre labels to capture specific conventions and audience expectations; subgenres inherit some features from parent genres while adding distinctive conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frye's classificatory system
rubrics_metrics.description: Northrop Frye classifies genres through the relation between the hero of the work and ourselves or the laws of nature, and by the juxtaposition of the 'real' and the 'ideal' to define romance, irony, comedy, and tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Frye's heuristic (hero vs. world; real vs. ideal) to interpret tone and mythic level; also consider Frye's audience-based division into drama (performed), lyric (sung), and epic (recited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre as culturally and historically situated
rubrics_metrics.description: Genres are defined by the general cultural movement of the historical period in which they were composed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualize genre labels historically; recognize that conventions and expectations shift with cultural movements (e.g., Romanticism, modernism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre conventions: style, mood, length, organizational features
rubrics_metrics.description: Genre categorizes literary works based on specific shared conventions, including style, mood, length, and organizational features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating work, identify the constellation of conventions (tone, pacing, narrative order, typical length) that signal a genre to readers and publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semi-fiction as a genre-mixing criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The genre of semi-fiction includes works that mix elements of both fiction and nonfiction, ranging from retellings of true stories with only names changed to fictional events with a semi-fictional protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how factual and fictional elements are balanced and signalled to readers; transparency about the blend affects genre assignment and reader expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiction vs. fable / medium-based restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: A commonly accepted distinction: the genre of 'fiction' is typically applied to prose texts (novels, novellas, short stories) and not to fables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign the label 'fiction' primarily to narrative prose forms, being careful with works (e.g., fables) that are traditional or didactic and may be categorized differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative classification axes (age and format)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other ways of categorizing books include age categories (adult, young adult, children's literature) and classification by format (graphic novels, picture books, radio plays).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these axes alongside genre to determine audience expectations and appropriate stylistic/formatting conventions for production and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama division (tragedy vs comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard division of drama into tragedy and comedy derives from Greek drama and continues to structure dramatic subgenres (including mixtures like tragicomedy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate dramatic works by their dominant tonal trajectory and structural conventions inherited from tragic/comic traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Character-related elements include antagonist, protagonist, character arc, character flaw, characterization techniques, foil, stock character, supporting character, false protagonist, unreliable narrator, and other role types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess characters for development (arc), plausibility, distinctiveness (voice, agency), and functional roles in plot and theme; consider common archetypes and how the work subverts or fulfills them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot and narrative structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot elements include conflict, exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, denouement, subplot, plot twist, cliffhanger, foreshadowing, flashback, and devices like Chekhov's gun or deus ex machina.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate narrative pacing, causal logic of events, use of plot devices, and the coherence of subplots; strong plots typically manage tension, escalation, and satisfying resolution (or deliberate non-resolution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting and worldbuilding
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting elements include fictional location (city, country, universe), alternate history, dystopia/utopia, fictional species, and worldbuilding details that establish verisimilitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the consistency, vividness, and functional integration of setting with plot and theme; worldbuilding should support story stakes without overwhelming narrative momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme, motif, and moral development
rubrics_metrics.description: Theme-related items include irony, leitmotif, metaphor, moral, moral development, motif, and recurring thematic structures (e.g., conflict between good and evil).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for coherent thematic development across plot and character, effective use of motifs and symbols, and whether the thematic material emerges organically rather than being didactic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style, diction, imagery, and rhetorical devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Stylistic elements include allegory, diction, figures of speech, imagery, mode, mood, narration, stylistic devices, symbolism, tone, and the guideline 'show, don't tell.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess sentence-level craft (word choice, imagery), rhetorical strategies, and the balance between showing and exposition; style should suit genre conventions and thematic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narration and point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative voice elements include first-person, second-person, third-person, third-person omniscient, subjectivity, unreliable narrator, multiple narrators, stream of consciousness, and breaking the fourth wall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate POV consistency, appropriateness to story scope, narrative reliability, and how the chosen voice shapes reader alignment and information flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and length distinctions (novel/novella/short story/flash/etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Major written forms include novel, novella, short story, drabble, sketch, flash fiction, and other form labels that often correspond to expected length and structural norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge work against formal expectations (e.g., compression for flash fiction, scope for novels) and whether the form serves the narrative intentions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devices, tropes, and cliché management
rubrics_metrics.description: Common devices and tropes listed include MacGuffin, red herring, trope, cliché, cliffhanger, parody, and other recurring conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify reliance on stock tropes or clichés; effective use often involves subversion, fresh framing, or purposeful invocation in service of theme or genre expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension of disbelief and verisimilitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Related concepts include suspension of disbelief and verisimilitude — maintaining a believable internal logic so readers accept the work's premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether narrative details and world rules are consistent enough to sustain reader immersion; unexplained contradictions or convenient coincidences can break suspension of disbelief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hook, pacing, and reader engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative techniques such as the 'hook', pacing, suspense, cliffhangers, and the management of tempo are listed under narrative techniques and structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the opening's ability to engage, pacing appropriateness to form/genre, and sustained engagement strategies (stakes, escalating conflict, reveal timing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue and dramatic speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue and related dramatic speech forms are included among narrative and stylistic devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess dialogue for distinctiveness of voice, economy (does it advance plot or reveal character), and realism appropriate to genre and context.
